what: Delta parallel robot (Clavel type). Three motors on the base, 120° apart, each drive a 48 mm upper arm through an 8:24 gear (3:1). From each arm a pair of parallel 56 mm lower links with ball joints runs down to a common tool head. The program solves the inverse kinematics for 13 XYZ waypoints: it lifts the head 10 mm, visits three stations 9.6 mm from the centre and 120° apart, dips 6 mm at each, and returns home. It runs the three motors together, scales their speeds so they arrive at the same time, and checks the head’s measured position after every move.
try: Open Vector with its program, press Reset, then Run straight away. The program starts only if all three motor encoders read within 5° of zero. If the simulation runs unpowered for a moment first, the arms sag under the head’s weight and this start guard stops the program; press Reset and Run again.
Waypoint 1 lifts the head straight up by 10 mm. Watch all three arms rise together by the same angle: about 15.5° at each shoulder, 46.5° at each motor.
Waypoints 2–10 visit the three stations. Compare the three arms: even a straight sideways move needs three different motor angles, about 43°, 35° and 49° at station 1.
Watch the tool head itself rather than the arms: it moves up, down and sideways but does not tilt or turn, because each pair of lower links forms a parallelogram.
why: Each pair of lower links forms a parallelogram, so the tool head cannot tilt; it can only translate in x, y and z. Three motors give exactly these three degrees of freedom. Each leg is solved on its own: the shoulder sits 200 LDU (80 mm) from the centre and the tool joints 60 LDU (24 mm), so the effective offset is 140 LDU. The elbow must lie on a circle of radius L = 48 mm around the shoulder and on a sphere of radius l = 56 mm around the tool joint. That gives D·cos θ + y·sin θ = (L² + q² − l²)/(2L), solved as θ = atan2(y, D) − acos K. The motor target is −3·(θ − 35°), because the gear multiplies by 3 and the saved pose has θ = 35°.
matters: Delta robots are the fast pick-and-place machines of packaging lines and the frame of many 3D printers: the heavy motors stay on the base and only light rods move. The price is a nonlinear, coupled relation between motor angles and tool position, and a workspace limited by the arm lengths. The program shows the standard answer: compute the inverse kinematics for every waypoint and scale the three motor speeds so they arrive together. In a headless run of the Brickwright simulator the tool head reached every waypoint within 0.23 mm of the program’s target, the shoulder angles matched the program’s inverse kinematics within 0.15°, and the head tilted by at most 0.06° during the whole run; that is a simulation observation, and no physical LEGO build has been tested.
question: The tool head rises straight up by 10 mm at the centre (waypoint 1). Do all three motors turn by the same angle? And when the head then moves 9.6 mm sideways to station 1?
answer: Straight up at the centre: yes. By symmetry each shoulder angle changes from 35° to about 19.5°, so all three motors turn by about +46.5°. Sideways to station 1: no. From the lifted pose the motor targets change by roughly −3.5° (A), −11.4° (B) and +3.0° (C). Even a straight sideways move needs three different motor motions, which is why the program scales the speeds so all three finish together.
further: Work through the leg equations by hand for waypoint 3 (x = −24, y = 192.47 LDU, z = 0) and check the three shoulder angles against the program’s 15°–40° guard.

Manual steering moves one motor at a time. Turn only motor A forward and predict where the head goes: up and towards arm A, while it stays level. Keeping each motor between 0° and 24° keeps the ideal head inside the program’s declared working box.
Compare Atlas Six (Stewart platform, six legs, six degrees of freedom) and Twinpoint (planar five-bar, two degrees of freedom): in all of them several chains share one end effector.

Limits: the simulation treats rods and ball joints as ideal. Real ball-joint play, rod flex and backlash in the 8:24 gears would appear as wobble of the head, and nothing here rates the payload or speed of a real build.
formula: Leg at angle φ: radial = x·cos φ + z·sin φ; D = 140 − radial; q² = x² + y² + z² + 140² − 280·radial; ρ = √(D² + y²); K = (L² + q² − l²)/(2Lρ) with L = 120 LDU (48 mm), l = 140 LDU (56 mm); θ = atan2(y, D) − acos K. Motor target = −3·(θ − 35°). Shoulders at φ = 90°, 330°, 210°. Coordinates in LDU, y downward.
